title: Cabin Noise Complaints in the Forward Premium Section — Request for a Quieter Divider Bay Treatment
abstract: Amaranth Airways reports a concentration of passenger noise complaints in the rows next to the forward cabin dividers and asks for a treatment that brings those seats into line with the rest of the premium cabin.

sections.request: Our premium cabin scores well everywhere except the two rows either side of the forward divider, where passengers keep telling us it is noticeably louder than the seats further back. Our cabin crew agree, and our own sound level readings taken in the cruise show a consistent difference between those rows and the middle of the same cabin. This is a commercial problem for us because those are seats we sell at the highest fare on the aircraft. We have looked behind the divider panels ourselves and there is very little in the way of treatment in the void above the panel line. We are not asking for a redesign of the cabin, only for something that can be fitted in that bay during a normal cabin refresh and that does not eat into the space we use for stowage.
sections.background: Sixty-one written complaints in twelve months, all naming the same seat rows. Our measurements show a difference of roughly four decibels between the divider rows and the reference position eight rows aft, taken in level cruise at typical weights. We have already replaced the divider panel seals on two aircraft with no measurable change. A previous request for an acoustic improvement in the lower hold was answered some years ago, so we know treatments of this kind exist.
sections.expected_outcome: A cabin treatment for the forward divider bays that removes the audible step between those rows and the rest of the cabin, fitted during a scheduled cabin visit, with no loss of stowage volume and no change to the certified emergency exit arrangements.

type_data.business_justification: Sixty-one complaints in a year against the highest-yield seats on the aircraft, with a measured four-decibel step that the operator considers a product defect rather than a comfort preference.
